title: Psalm 67: Let All the Peoples Praise You
summary: Echoing the priestly blessing, the psalmist asks God to be gracious to his people and make his face shine on them, so that God's ways and salvation will be known among all nations. A refrain calls all peoples to praise God, who judges them justly and guides them. The psalm ends with a harvest gathered and a prayer that God's blessing will lead the ends of the earth to fear him.
story: Psalm 67 is the shortest of the four praise psalms in 65 to 68, and it may be the most outward-looking psalm in Book II. Psalm 65 celebrated God's gift of harvest, and Psalm 66 called all the earth to praise; Psalm 67 joins those themes and makes the point explicit: God blesses Israel so that the nations will come to know him. This is the promise God made to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), turned into a prayer. Psalm 68, which follows, will describe God's triumphant procession and the kings of the earth bringing him gifts.
historical:
The heading names no author and calls the psalm both a psalm and a song, with stringed instruments. It gives no occasion, but verse 6, “The earth has yielded its harvest,” suggests it was sung at a harvest festival, perhaps the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), which celebrated the wheat harvest, or the Feast of Booths in the autumn. Some scholars read verse 6 as a prayer for a future harvest rather than thanks for one already gathered; the Hebrew verb form allows either reading.

The psalm's date is uncertain. Its universal vision, with all nations praising Israel's God, has led some scholars to date it after the exile, when prophets such as Isaiah 40 to 66 spoke of the nations coming to God. Others note that the promise to bless the nations goes back to Abraham, and that such hopes were part of Israel's faith from early on. The psalm could have been used in many periods.
cultural:
The opening line takes up the priestly blessing that God gave Aaron and his sons to speak over Israel: the LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his face toward you and give you peace (Numbers 6:24-26). Israel's priests pronounced this blessing in worship, and the psalm echoes its words, changing it from you to us and from the LORD to God.

The image of a face shining toward someone meant favor and goodwill, like a king's face lighting up with approval when a subject came before him (Proverbs 16:15). A hidden face meant displeasure or absence. In an agricultural society, God's blessing was seen most concretely in the harvest, and a good yield was taken as a sign of God's favor. The psalm takes that ordinary sign of blessing and gives it a global purpose: when the nations see God blessing Israel, they will come to know and fear him.
literary: Psalm 67 is carefully built in a mirror pattern. Verses 1 and 2 (the prayer for blessing so that the nations may know God) correspond to verses 6 and 7 (the harvest and blessing so that the ends of the earth may fear him). Verses 3 and 5 are an identical refrain: “Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You.” At the center, verse 4 gives the reason: God judges the peoples justly and leads the nations. The structure places God's just rule over all nations at the heart of the psalm. The words for peoples and nations appear again and again, underlining the psalm's universal concern. Selah appears after verses 1 and 4.

outline.t: Bless us, so that Your ways may be known on earth
Refrain: let all the peoples praise You
The nations rejoice under God's just rule
Refrain: let all the peoples praise You
Harvest and blessing, so that the ends of the earth fear him

doctrines.note: The psalm prays for blessing not for Israel's sake alone but so that God's ways and salvation will be known among all nations. God's blessing on his people is meant to flow outward to the world.
The echo of the priestly blessing and the promise to Abraham ties the psalm to God's covenant with Israel. That covenant was always meant to bring blessing to the nations.

Verse 4 describes God judging the peoples justly and leading the nations of the earth. God is king not only of Israel but of all peoples, and the psalm looks forward to the day when all acknowledge his rule.

words.note: Chanan, to be gracious, to show favor. It is the first verb of the psalm and a key word of the priestly blessing. It describes undeserved kindness freely given. God's grace to his people is the starting point of the blessing that reaches the nations.

Or, to shine, to give light. The prayer that God will cause his face to shine on his people comes from the priestly blessing. A shining face is a sign of favor and delight; the image is of God looking at his people with pleasure.

Yeshuah, salvation. Verse 2 prays that God's salvation will be known among all nations. The word can mean rescue, deliverance, or victory. The name Jesus (Yeshua in Hebrew) is built from the same root, which Christian readers have long noticed, though the psalm itself uses the word in its ordinary sense.

Barakh, to bless. It appears in the first line and twice at the end (verses 6 and 7). Blessing is God's gift of life, abundance, and favor, and the psalm frames it as a means rather than an end: God blesses us so that all the ends of the earth will fear him.

christ: Paul says that Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying that all nations would be blessed in him (Galatians 3:8). Psalm 67 prays for exactly that. In the New Testament, the blessing reaches the nations through Jesus Christ, the descendant of Abraham, in whom God's face shines on the world (2 Corinthians 4:6). When the aged Simeon held the infant Jesus in the temple, he praised God for a salvation prepared in the sight of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:30-32). The church's mission to the nations is the answer to this psalm's prayer. The psalm is not a direct prophecy of Christ, but its hope is fulfilled in him.
questions: The psalm prays for blessing so that God's ways will be known on earth. How might God's blessings in your life be meant for others?
What does it mean for God's face to shine on you? When have you sensed his favor?
The refrain calls all the peoples to praise God. How does this psalm shape the way you think about people of other nations and cultures?
